identification.bodyShape: Oblong, laterally compressed body with a large mouth reaching below the middle of the eye; a stout, robust reef bass rather than a slender one.
identificationTraits: Caudal fin has three lobes formed by long, pointed upper, middle, and lower rays - a trilobed tail rather than a simple fork or square edge.
Dorsal fin has 10 spines (front spines longest) and 11 soft rays, with membranes between the spines deeply notched.
Gill cover bears three flat spines.
Anal fin has 3 spines and 7 soft rays.
Pale blue-to-white spot in the center of each scale forms faint longitudinal stripe rows along the sides.
White spots and bands mark the dorsal fin.
identification.coloration: Smoky gray, dusky brown, or blue-black on the back and sides fading paler toward the belly, with rows of pale scale-center spots and a white-marked dorsal fin.
identification.spawningColoration: Dominant, spawning-capable males develop a bright blue-to-green nuchal hump and coloring around the eyes and nape. This is a physiological marker of sex and social status, not a targeting cue.
identification.adultAppearance: A stout, dark, structure-associated bass with a trilobed tail, deeply notched dorsal fin, and rows of pale scale spots; large dominant males show a blue head hump.
identification.sexualDimorphism: Protogynous hermaphrodite. Females typically mature around 7.5 in, males around 9 in; dominant males are larger and develop the blue nuchal hump, while subordinate males lack it. Size, not a fixed external marker, is the main field cue to likely sex.
identification.averageAdultLength: Commonly encountered fish run smaller than the species maximum; typical length in most sources is well under 20 in.
identification.commonAnglingSize: Legal-size fish are commonly in the 12-16 in range where minimum sizes require roughly 11-13 in, varying by state and stock.
identification.typicalWeight: Most landed fish are well under the documented maximum of about 6 lb.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Up to about 24 in and 6 lb per ASMFC life-history summary; NOAA Fisheries cites growth to about 2 ft and 9 lb.
identification.longevity: Females to about 8 years, males to about 12 years (NOAA Fisheries); ASMFC gives a species maximum near 20 years with fish over 9 years uncommon. Sources do not fully agree on the upper bound.

gaps: No agency or peer-reviewed source was found contrasting black sea bass against similar-looking Centropristis or serranid species (e.g. bank sea bass); similarSpecies left empty rather than guessed.
Longevity figures disagree between NOAA Fisheries (8/12 yr by sex) and ASMFC (~20 yr max) - recorded rather than resolved.
No single continent-wide average adult length figure was found; only maximum-size figures are well sourced.

social.byLifeStage: Adults associate loosely around shared structure (reefs, wrecks, oyster bottom) rather than schooling in open water; social structure includes size-based dominance among males.
social.note: Fish concentrate on productive hard bottom and structure, which reads as loose aggregation rather than either strict schooling or solitary behavior.

feedingStrategy.note: Opportunistic, visually-oriented predator that takes crabs, shrimp, worms, small fish, and clams as available from structure and adjacent soft bottom.

behavior.territoriality: Dominant males defend a home range and a group of females rather than holding a fixed ambush point the way a solitary predator does; reported male home ranges are on the order of a fraction of a square kilometer to several square kilometers.

dielTendency.note: Sources describe daytime association with structure and foraging that extends onto surrounding open/soft bottom; no agency or peer-reviewed source made a strong nocturnal-vs-diurnal claim for this species, so it is recorded as mixed rather than assigned confidently.

behavior.seasonalActivity: Activity tracks the seasonal inshore/offshore migration below. Fish are most catchable on shallow nearshore structure during the warm season; cold-season fish are offshore and deep.
behavior.thermalDrivenBehavior: Migration is temperature-triggered: fish move off the nearshore shelf as bottom temperatures decline in fall (roughly the 10-12°C / low-40s-to-50s°F range in one source, or a 7°C threshold in another) and return inshore as temperatures climb in spring. Near 6°C (about 43°F), sources describe adults becoming inactive and sheltering in holes and crevices rather than actively feeding.
behavior.depthMovement: Ontogenetic and seasonal: young-of-year settle in shallow nearshore/estuarine habitat; older juveniles and adults occupy progressively deeper water offshore in winter (240-540 ft reported for the Mid-Atlantic stock) and shallower nearshore structure (commonly under 120 ft) in the warm season.
behavior.predatorAvoidance: Uses hard structure - reefs, wrecks, rock, oyster bottom - as primary cover; no source describes an additional predator-avoidance behavior beyond structure use.
behavior.coverUse: Irregular hard bottom, reefs, wrecks, rock piles, jetties, pilings, and oyster bottom are the consistently cited holding structures across sources.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Protogynous hermaphrodite: most individuals begin life as females, and a portion transition to male as they grow, generally between about 2 and 5 years of age - a size/age-driven process, not a seasonal event in itself. Reported spawning windows differ by stock and source (South Atlantic stock February-May per SAFMC; Mid-Atlantic stock May-July extending into fall per ASMFC, or June-October per NOAA Fisheries), with spawning habitat generally described only in general terms as inner continental shelf depths. This is biological and conservation context only; it does not describe a place or a time to fish.

gaps: No source gave a clear day-vs-night feeding claim strong enough to classify diel tendency beyond 'mixed'.
Cold-front, water-clarity, and angling-pressure response were not addressed in any agency or peer-reviewed source found and are omitted rather than inferred.
Exact migration trigger temperature disagrees slightly between sources (approx. 7°C in one, 10-12°C in another) and is reported as a range rather than resolved to one figure.

diet.primaryNote: Generalist bottom-and-structure feeder. Sources consistently list crabs, shrimp, small fish, worms (polychaetes), and clams/mussels/razor clams; one peer-reviewed diet study found arthropods (crabs and other decapods) as the largest single prey category. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current feeding event.

lifeStageDiet.juvenile: Smaller fish (under about 20 cm per the cited diet study) feed almost exclusively on crustaceans - amphipods, sand shrimp, and small rock crabs.
lifeStageDiet.adult: Larger fish add more fish prey (e.g. sand lance) to a diet still dominated by crabs and other decapod crustaceans, plus worms and mollusks.

diet.ontogeneticShift: Diet shifts from an almost purely crustacean diet in smaller/younger fish toward a mixed crustacean-and-fish diet as fish grow larger and gape increases.
diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity (what the species is documented to eat) is not proof that a feeding event is happening now. Observed current forage still comes from a user observation or Hatch Match, never from this record alone.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Black sea bass behavior is dominated by a temperature-driven inshore/offshore migration rather than a spawning-timed pattern: warm-season fish hold shallow nearshore structure, cold-season fish move to deep outer-shelf water. Spawning and sex change are biological/conservation context and are not treated as a seasonal target window.

entries.habitatClass: Deep outer continental shelf, well offshore of the nearshore reefs and wrecks used the rest of the year.
entries.depthTendency: Reported as deep as 240-540 ft for the Mid-Atlantic stock in winter.
entries.thermalContext: Fish move here as bottom temperatures fall; near 6°C (about 43°F) sources describe adults becoming inactive and sheltering rather than feeding.
invalidators: treating shallow nearshore wrecks as productive winter water for this species in the Mid-Atlantic stock

entries.habitatClass: Return migration onto nearshore hard structure - reefs, wrecks, rock, jetties, pilings, oyster bottom - as bottom water warms.
entries.movementTendency: Spring return migration is described as faster and more directed than the fall offshore movement.
entries.conservationNote: South Atlantic stock spawning window (February-May, per SAFMC) overlaps this season. Included as biology only - not a location or timing target.
entries.presentationImplication: Bottom contact and drop presentations over reviewed nearshore structure classes as fish reoccupy shallow reefs and wrecks.
invalidators: reading spawning-season timing as a bite window

entries.habitatClass: Shallow nearshore structure, commonly under 120 ft in the Mid-Atlantic stock.
entries.depthTendency: Shallowest seasonal depths of the year.
entries.conservationNote: Mid-Atlantic stock spawning window (May-October depending on source) overlaps this season. Included as biology only.
entries.presentationImplication: Bottom contact, drop presentation, and structure-vertical over nearshore reef, wreck, and rock-pile classes.
invalidators: assuming a spawning-season closure applies without checking the current state/stock rule

entries.habitatClass: Fish begin leaving shallow nearshore structure for the outer shelf as bottom temperatures decline.
entries.movementTendency: Offshore migration begins as bottom temperature approaches roughly 10-12°C (about 50-54°F) in one source, or a 7°C threshold in another.
invalidators: treating fall as a fixed calendar date rather than a temperature-triggered movement
